It differs from non-view-dependent isocontouring by skipping internal sections that are occluded by the external isosurface, and from Greene's method by marking triangles as visible in software and forwarding them to graphics hardware for final visibility determination rather than rendering the visible portion in software [S1, book].

The claim is fully supported by the provided text. The first part of the claim ('differs from non-view-dependent isocontouring by skipping internal sections that are occluded by the external isosurface') is supported by the passage stating that in view-dependent methods, 'only the solid lines are extracted, whereas in non-view-dependent isocontouring, both solid and dotted are extracted,' and that internal sections are 'occluded by other sections of the isosurface.' The second part of the claim ('differs from Greene's method by marking triangles as visible in software and forwarding them to graphics hardware for final visibility determination rather than rendering the visible portion in software') is explicitly supported by the section 'Hierarchical Visibility Mask,' which states: 'Our implementation differs from the one proposed by Greene in that we do not actually render the visible portion of a visible triangle. Rather, we mark the triangle as visible and forward it to the graphics hardware. It is then left to the graphics accelerator to determine which pieces of the triangle are actually visible and correctly render them.'
